definition: The empirical rule that the frequency of a word is roughly inversely proportional to its rank in the corpus.
details: In natural language the most common word appears about twice as often as the second most common, three times as often as the third, and so on. Zipfian (power-law) structure appears throughout text and explains why tokenizers work well and why long-tail words are rare — an important fact when modeling language.

explainer.lead: Zipf's Law is the empirical rule that a word's frequency is roughly inversely proportional to its rank in a corpus. It explains why tokenizers work well and why long-tail words are rare, an important fact when modeling language.

tiers.eli5: Like a party where the most popular guest is talked to twice as much as the second most popular, three times as much as the third, and so on down the list.
tiers.practitioner: Engineers rely on Zipfian structure when designing tokenizers and estimating how often rare words appear. A pitfall is expecting uniform word frequencies when the distribution is long-tailed.
tiers.paperLevel: Frequency is roughly inversely proportional to rank: the most common word appears about twice as often as the second, three times as often as the third, and so on.

explainer.example: In a corpus the most common word appears about twice as often as the second most common and three times as often as the third.

citation.title: Power laws, Pareto distributions and Zipf’s law
